name: English
title: Free DISC Personality Test — Online, 10 Minutes, No Sign-Up
description: Free DISC personality test: 24 questions, 10 minutes, no sign-up. Find your dominant style, strengths and growth areas. Instant result, also by email.

addon.D: more drive, speed and readiness to take responsibility
addon.I: more sociability, optimism and the ability to inspire people
addon.S: more patience, reliability and attention to the team
addon.C: more precision, caution and reliance on facts

blocks.I: I like being the center of attention

blocks.D: I say exactly what I think
I get straight to the point

blocks.S: I accept things as they are

strengths: You make decisions quickly and take responsibility for them
You keep your footing in a crisis and act when others hesitate
You set ambitious goals and achieve them
growth: Impatience with people who work more slowly or carefully
A tendency to push a decision through without hearing alternatives
Bluntness that others experience as pressure
motivation: Authority and the ability to influence how things go
D.stress: Under pressure you become harder and less tolerant: you interrupt, take everything on yourself and bypass rules for the sake of speed. Clear authority and room to act independently help.
communication: Keep it short and to the point: results, deadlines, options
Don't drag out the introduction or beat around the bush
Offer a choice rather than a ready-made answer: deciding for themselves matters
D.environment: A dynamic environment with a lot of autonomy, clear goals and a direct link between effort and results. Routine and tight supervision are demotivating.

strengths: You connect with people easily and win them over
You inspire and motivate the team
You generate ideas and see opportunities where others see problems
You stay optimistic in difficult situations
growth: Promises made in the heat of the moment that are hard to keep later
Not enough attention to details and deadlines
A tendency to talk more than listen
I.stress: Under pressure you become scattered and impulsive, avoid unpleasant conversations and may overestimate how things stand. Open discussion and support from colleagues help.
communication: Start with a personal connection, not the agenda
Give room to speak up and discuss ideas
Put agreements in writing: it helps both sides
I.environment: An open, friendly environment with plenty of contact, recognition and freedom from rigid procedures. Isolation and monotony drain the energy.

strengths: You can be relied on over the long haul
You know how to listen to and support others
You bring the team together and defuse conflicts
growth: Resistance to change, even beneficial change
Difficulty saying no and standing your ground
Keeping disagreement to yourself to preserve the peace
motivation: Clear expectations and rules of the game
S.stress: Under pressure you withdraw, become overly accommodating and put off decisions. Sudden change and open conflict are especially hard to bear. Time to adjust and a calm conversation help.
communication: Give advance notice of changes and explain why they are needed
Ask for their opinion directly: they rarely volunteer it
Don't push or rush them for an answer
S.environment: A stable environment with clear processes, good relationships and a reasonable pace of change. Chaos, constant switching and aggressive competition are exhausting.

strengths: High quality of work and attention to detail
The ability to think through risks and plan ahead
growth: Perfectionism and missed deadlines in pursuit of the ideal
Excessive criticism of yourself and others
Retreating into analysis instead of acting
C.stress: Under pressure you withdraw into yourself, become overly critical and get stuck in details. Having to act without data is irritating. Clear criteria and time to verify help.
communication: Allow time to think it over; don't demand an answer right away
Criticize specifically and on the merits, without emotion
C.environment: A structured environment with clear standards, access to information and the ability to work with focus. Uncertainty, haste and emotional pressure reduce effectiveness.

D.name: Achiever
D.summary: You move toward the goal directly and fast: you take the initiative, decide without lengthy discussion and aren't afraid of resistance. Being in control and seeing measurable results matters to you.
careers: Head of a department or project
D.team: Takes the lead even when nobody appointed them, sets goals and pushes the team toward results. Indispensable when an unpopular decision has to be made or a project pulled out of a crisis. With them the team moves fast, but not always comfortably: make sure the cautious voices are heard too.

with.D: With another D, divide areas of responsibility in advance and argue about criteria, not about who's in charge.
with.I: Give the person two minutes before getting down to business, and acknowledge their contribution out loud.
with.S: Slow down, give warning of changes, and wait for the answer to your question without filling the pause.
with.C: Back your decisions with facts and allow time for checking: for a C that isn't stalling, it's the job.

I.name: Inspirer
I.summary: You work through people: you make connections easily, spread enthusiasm and persuade with words and mood. Recognition and lively interaction matter to you, while formalities and routine wear you out quickly.
I.team: Creates mood and connections: introduces people, lifts gloom, is first to suggest ideas and first to volunteer to present them to the outside world. With them the team is livelier and the presentations more persuasive. They benefit from a partner who watches deadlines and details, otherwise enthusiasm drifts away from the facts.

with.D: Keep it short and to the point, start with the result, and save the emotions for later.
with.I: Agree on who takes notes, and end the conversation with a to-do list and deadlines.
with.S: Don't change plans on the fly, and ask for their opinion directly: an S won't push it on you.
with.C: Prepare the facts, allow time to think, and don't take checking of the details for a refusal.

S.name: Anchor
S.summary: You create stability: you keep your word, finish what you start, support people and smooth over conflicts. Predictability, trust and time to get used to change matter to you.
careers: Operational and service roles with steady processes
S.team: The one you can rely on: sees things through, remembers agreements, helps newcomers and smooths over conflicts. Often holds the team together without anyone noticing. Risks going unrecognized and being overloaded with other people's tasks because they can't say no.

with.D: Voice disagreement right away and briefly; ask for clear priorities instead of guessing.
with.I: State your boundaries out loud and ask for a plan: one idea isn't enough for you.
with.S: Set deadlines for each other and take turns being the one who decides.
with.C: Take remarks as care for quality, and propose changes in small steps.

C.name: Analyst
C.summary: You rely on facts and standards: you check, analyze, plan and dislike hasty decisions. Quality and being right matter to you more than speed and outward effect.
C.team: Makes sure what gets done actually works: checks, finds mistakes before clients do, and plans for risks. With them the team is more accurate but slower. They should explain the logic of their requirements to colleagues and sometimes settle for “good enough”.

with.D: Offer a “good enough now” option and report risks briefly, with consequences.
with.I: Start by acknowledging the idea, and explain your conclusions in plain words.
with.S: Soften criticism and notice their contribution out loud: for an S, the atmosphere is part of the result.
with.C: Decide on a sufficient level of quality in advance and limit the time for analysis.

DI.name: Pioneer
DI.summary: Drive and charm: you lead quickly toward the goal and know how to bring people along. You persuade with momentum and enthusiasm and decide on the go, but patience for details and caution often run short.
careers: Head of new product and market launches
DI.team: The launcher: sets an ambitious goal, finds allies and leads the way. Indispensable at the start of a project and in negotiations that call for drive and charm at once. Over the long haul they need colleagues with S and C who will see things through and check the details.

with.D: Divide spheres of influence and don't compete for attention: two leaders need different fronts.
with.I: Ride the shared enthusiasm, but end with a to-do list with owners and deadlines.
with.S: Ease off the pressure, give warning of changes, and don't take silence for agreement.
with.C: Give them facts and time: a C isn't slowing you down, they're insuring your pace against mistakes.

DC.name: Strategist
DC.summary: Results through quality: you are demanding of yourself and others, think systematically and never decide without arguments. Strong on complex tasks, but you can come across as cold and overly critical.
careers: Head of an engineering or analytics team
DC.team: Combines drive and quality: sets a high bar and reaches it, thinks in systems, sees risks before others do. With them the team is focused and productive, but may feel coldness and constant evaluation. They should acknowledge people's contributions more often and explain decisions rather than only make demands.

with.D: Argue about facts and criteria; agree on who has the last word in contested areas.
with.I: Listen to ideas all the way through before taking them apart, and praise in public.
with.S: Explain why changes are needed and thank them for their reliability: an S won't ask.
with.C: Decide where speed is needed and where precision, and don't push on deadlines in the quality zone.

DS.name: Practitioner
DS.summary: Persistence and reliability: you push steadily toward the goal without any fuss and finish what you start. You value independence and stability at the same time, which is a rare combination.
careers: Middle manager in a large company
DS.team: The workhorse: takes a task and carries it through to the result without fuss, doesn't abandon it halfway, keeps their word. A rare combination of independence and reliability makes them a manager's mainstay. From the outside they can seem stubborn and closed; they should talk through their plans more often and hear out other options.

with.D: Agree on the goal and the deadline, and keep the route to yourself: micromanagement demotivates you.
with.I: Don't wave ideas away as chatter, but ask for a concrete plan.
with.S: Take the decision on yourself, but explain it and give time to adjust.
with.C: Acknowledge the value of checking and agree on the criteria for “done” in advance.

ID.name: Motivator
ID.summary: Energy and drive: you infect people with ideas and aren't afraid to take the initiative. You easily sell ideas and goals, but risk overestimating your strength and underestimating the details.
careers: Head of a sales or marketing team
ID.team: Energizes and leads: spreads ideas, lifts the mood, isn't afraid of initiative or the spotlight. Great where many people need to be persuaded and inspired at once. Risks overestimating their strength and promising more than is possible, so they need a partner in charge of reality: deadlines, resources, details.

with.D: Keep it short, with the result up front; a D's drive isn't hostility, it's speed.
with.I: End the meeting with written agreements, or enthusiasm will drift away from the work.
with.S: Give warning of changes and don't decide for an S: ask for their opinion directly.
with.C: Prepare the numbers and allow time for an answer: a C's silence is thinking, not refusal.

IS.name: Mentor
IS.summary: Warmth and involvement: you win people over, and know how to support and unite them. Relationships and atmosphere matter to you, while conflict and harsh demands are hard to take.
careers: HR business partner, onboarding and training
Head of a service or close-knit team
IS.team: The one people go to talk to: listens, supports, connects people and keeps the atmosphere. With them the team is friendlier and more resilient. Tough decisions and unpleasant conversations come hard; they should remember that honest feedback is a form of care too.

with.D: Talk business briefly and don't be hurt by directness; voice disagreement right away.
with.I: Support the ideas, but ask for a plan and deadlines, or you'll both get carried away.
with.S: Name problems out loud and set deadlines for each other: without that, nothing moves.
with.C: Take criticism of the details as care for quality, not as being about you.

IC.name: Presenter
IC.summary: Eloquence and precision: you can convincingly present a well-thought-out position. You combine sociability with attention to facts, but may waver between spontaneity and caution.
careers: Teacher, lecturer, author of training materials
IC.team: Knows how to explain: turns the complex into the clear and presents a well-considered position convincingly. Useful at the junction between experts and the audience. Wavers between “say it” and “check it”, which can delay decisions; a clear agreement on when speed is needed and when precision helps.

with.D: Start with the conclusion; keep the details and reasoning ready, but don't open with them.
with.I: Enjoy the common language, but record who does what and by when.
with.S: Don't change plans on the fly, and ask for their opinion directly, giving time to answer.
with.C: Speak the language of data and settle for “good enough” where the cost of a mistake is low.

SI.name: Diplomat
SI.summary: Calm and friendliness: you create an atmosphere of trust, smooth over rough edges and support the team. Saying no and defending an unpopular decision is hard for you.
careers: Support for projects with many participants
SI.team: Builds trust: calm, friendly, attentive to everyone, smooths over rough edges and helps people reach agreement. With them the team has fewer conflicts. Finds it hard to say “no” and to defend an unpopular decision; they should learn to express disagreement before it builds up.

with.D: Voice disagreement right away and briefly: a D respects directness more than compliance.
with.I: State your boundaries and ask for specifics: one idea isn't enough.
with.S: Take turns taking the initiative, and don't put off difficult conversations.
with.C: Ask them to explain the logic of a rule, and propose changes in small steps.

SC.name: Specialist
SC.summary: Reliability and accuracy: you work methodically, follow the rules and see things through without haste. You value stability and clear expectations, while abrupt change and pressure are hard to bear.
SC.team: The keeper of order: works methodically, follows the rules, sees things through, remembers how it was done last time. Processes rest on them. Abrupt change and pressure are hard to take; the team should involve them in changes early, and they themselves should speak up about overload rather than endure it.

with.D: Ask for clear priorities and report risks briefly, with consequences.
with.I: Don't mistake enthusiasm for a plan: ask for deadlines and owners.
with.S: Set deadlines for each other and name problems out loud, even small ones.
with.C: Decide on a sufficient level of quality in advance, or you'll both drown in details.

SD.name: Implementer
SD.summary: Perseverance and patience: you calmly but firmly drive things to a result without getting caught up in needless discussion. Reliable over the long haul, though from the outside you may seem stubborn.
careers: Owner of a small, stable business
SD.team: Gets to the result calmly and firmly: no rush, no needless discussion, but no retreat either. Reliable over the long haul, not afraid of responsibility. From the outside they can seem stubborn; they should explain their decisions and let colleagues influence them.

with.D: Agree on the goal and the deadline; choose the method yourself, and don't put up with micromanagement in silence.
with.I: Listen to the ideas, but ask for a plan: your firmness will help an I see things through.
with.S: Take the decision on yourself, but explain it and give time to adjust.
with.C: Agree on the criteria for “done” in advance and respect the time needed for checking.

CD.name: Perfectionist
CD.summary: Standards and willpower: you demand precision from yourself and others, spot mistakes quickly and aren't afraid to point them out. Strong on complex expert tasks, but you can be too strict and closed off.
CD.team: The quality guarantee: sees mistakes before anyone else, demands precision and isn't afraid to say so. With them the team does better work, but may feel under constant inspection. They should start with what was done well and explain the criteria beforehand, not afterward.

with.D: Report risks briefly, with an assessment of the consequences; offer a “good enough now” option.
with.I: Start by acknowledging the idea; make criticism specific and not harsh.
with.S: Soften your remarks and notice their contribution out loud: coldness wounds an S more than it seems.
with.C: Limit the time for analysis and decide in advance where to stop.

CS.name: Expert
CS.summary: Precision and consistency: you work thoughtfully, check the details and rely on proven methods. A dependable specialist who finds uncertainty and rapid change hard to handle.
CS.team: The reliable specialist: works thoughtfully, checks details, relies on proven methods and doesn't let people down. The team trusts their conclusions. Uncertainty and rapid change are hard on them; it helps when changes are explained in advance and when a considered answer, not an instant reaction, is expected of them.

with.D: Ask for time to check, but name the date by which you'll give an answer.
with.I: Explain your conclusions in plain words and don't mistake an I's emotions for flippancy.
with.S: Discuss changes in small steps and don't criticize in front of others.
with.C: Agree in advance on what level of detail is sufficient.

CI.name: Consultant
CI.summary: Analysis and connection: you can get to the bottom of a question and explain it to others in plain terms. A rare combination: caution in conclusions and ease in communication. Sometimes the inner tug-of-war between "verify" and "share" gets in the way.
careers: Author of training materials and documentation
CI.team: The translator between experts and everyone else: understands the subject and can explain it so people get it. Valuable where things need both checking and persuading. The inner tension between “check it” and “share it” sometimes slows things down; an agreement on when a preliminary conclusion is enough helps.

with.D: Start with the conclusion; keep the reasoning ready, but don't open with it.
with.I: You'll find a common language easily; make sure the conversation ends in a plan.
with.S: Don't change your conclusions on the fly, and allow time: an S needs predictability.
with.C: Speak the language of data, but don't argue over every detail.

disc.title: What Is DISC: The Model, the Four Behavioral Styles and How to Read a Profile
disc.description: A plain-language guide to DISC: where the model comes from, what it measures, the four styles D, I, S, C, how the score is calculated and how to read your profile.
disc.lead: DISC is a behavioral model that describes how a person acts, communicates and makes decisions on four scales: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness and Conscientiousness. It is neither an IQ test nor a diagnosis, but a shared language for talking about behavioral styles.

p: The foundation was laid by American psychologist William Marston in his book Emotions of Normal People (1928). He described four types of reaction that depend on whether a person sees the environment as favorable or hostile and feels stronger or weaker than the circumstances. That gave four dimensions: Dominance, Inducement (later Influence), Submission (later Steadiness) and Compliance (Conscientiousness).

Marston himself never built a questionnaire. The first instruments based on his model appeared in the 1950s–1970s (Walter Clarke, John Geier), and today dozens of versions exist. The name DiSC® with a lowercase “i” is a trademark of the publisher Wiley; our test is an independent, open version built on the same four-factor model.

It helps to picture the model as two axes. The first is pace: some people act fast and assertively, others deliberately and cautiously. The second is focus: some concentrate on tasks and results, others on people and relationships. Crossing the axes gives four styles: D is fast pace and task focus, I is fast pace and people focus, S is deliberate pace and people focus, C is deliberate pace and task focus.
Everyone has all four styles; only the proportion differs. A profile shows which styles show up most often in your habitual work behavior and which take effort.

D, Dominance: results, control, speed, readiness for conflict. I, Influence: communication, enthusiasm, the ability to bring people along. S, Steadiness: support, reliability, patience, stability. C, Conscientiousness: accuracy, quality, rules, reliance on facts.

A detailed description of each style, with traits, strengths, growth areas, motivation and the best way to communicate with it, is on the Four Styles page. Combinations of a dominant and a secondary style produce 16 profiles, each with its own page.

sections.h: How the test works and how the score is calculated
p: The test has 24 blocks of four statements. In each block you mark one statement that describes you most and one that describes you least. Every statement belongs to one of the four styles.

For each style, the score is the number of “most” marks minus the number of “least” marks: from −24 to +24. The style with the highest score becomes dominant. A secondary style counts if its score is positive and at least 40% of the dominant one (minimum 3 points). The chart shows three lines: the public self (“most” marks), the natural self (“least” marks, inverted) and the overall profile.

The dominant style is your habitual way of acting, the one that switches on automatically. The secondary style adds a shade: for example, a D with a secondary I persuades with momentum and enthusiasm, while a D with a secondary C persuades with demands and arguments. Values above the midpoint (50%) are considered pronounced.

No profile is good or bad: every style has strengths and growth areas. Nor is it a verdict: behavior depends on context, role and experience, so results at work and at home may differ, and a profile can shift in a year or two. A balanced profile, where no style stands out, usually indicates flexibility and, less often, uncertain answers.

Teams use DISC to understand why colleagues react differently and to agree on communication rules. For managers the model helps adapt their leadership style: some people need freedom and challenge, others clear expectations and time to adjust. In sales and negotiation, DISC suggests how to speak to a person in their own language.
In recruiting, DISC works as an interview topic and a reference point, but not as the sole basis for a decision: the model describes behavioral preferences, not competence or fit for a role.

DISC is a self-report: the result reflects how you see yourself and depends on honesty and mood. A short questionnaire gives an orientation, not a precise measurement, so treat the profile as a starting point for reflection and conversation rather than a diagnosis. If the result seems off, take the test again, answering quickly and with work situations in mind.

The links lead to the originals or to the article records in academic databases.

faq.title: DISC Test FAQ — Frequently Asked Questions
faq.description: Answers to common questions: how long the DISC test takes, whether it is free, how accurate it is, what D, I, S, C stand for, whether a team can take it and where the result goes.
faq.lead: Short answers to what people most often ask before the test and after the result.

items.q: How long does the test take?
items.a: The test has 24 blocks of four statements. It usually takes 8–12 minutes. Don't overthink it: your first reaction is the most accurate, and you can change a choice until you press “Next”.
Yes, completely: no sign-up, no hidden charges and no paid “extended reports”. The result appears on screen right after the last block and is emailed to the address you provide.

items.q: What do the letters D, I, S, C mean?
items.a: D is Dominance (results and control), I is Influence (people and enthusiasm), S is Steadiness (support and stability), C is Conscientiousness (accuracy and quality). Everyone has all four styles, but to different degrees.

DISC is a self-report, so accuracy depends on how honestly you answered and whether you thought about your real behavior at work rather than the behavior you would like. A short questionnaire gives a reliable indication of your dominant style, but not a precise measurement. If you doubt the result, take the test again in a few days.

items.q: What is a secondary style, and what are profiles like DI or SC?
items.a: The dominant style is the one with the highest score. If the second-highest style is also pronounced (at least 40% of the dominant one), it counts as secondary and adds its shade. That gives 16 profiles: four pure ones (D, I, S, C) and twelve combinations such as DI or SC.

No style stands out noticeably. Most often this means behavioral flexibility: you switch between styles easily depending on the situation. Sometimes it reflects uncertain answers. Try taking the test again, answering faster and with a specific work role in mind.

items.q: Can a whole team take the test?
items.a: Yes. Send your colleagues the link to the site; on the result screen each of them gets a link and a code, so ask them to forward those to you. In the admin panel (link in the footer) the codes are collected into a table you can copy into Excel. The table is stored only in your browser.

items.q: Where does the result go and who can see it?
items.a: The result is shown on screen, saved in your browser and sent to the email address you entered before the test. Nobody else sees it unless you share the report link yourself. See the Privacy page for details.

items.q: Can I take the test again?
items.a: Yes, at any time: press “Take the test again” on the result screen. A profile can change with role, experience and circumstances, so it is useful to compare results after a year.

items.q: How is DISC different from MBTI and the Big Five?
items.a: DISC describes observable behavior at work on four scales and works well for team conversations. MBTI sorts people into 16 preference types. The Big Five is the scientific standard for measuring personality traits, but its results are harder to turn into practical recommendations. The models don't contradict each other; they answer different questions.

items.q: Is this the full version of the DISC test?
items.a: Yes. This is the classic full “most like me / least like me” form: 24 blocks of four statements, 96 in total, one per style in each block. There are versions with 28 blocks or with 40 scale-rated questions: they differ in format, but the model and the four styles are the same. There are no shortened “demos” on this site; the result is calculated from all 24 blocks.

No. The test doesn't check knowledge and doesn't measure how “good” an employee you are: it describes your habitual behavioral style. Any attempt to answer “the right way” only distorts the profile. The only correct approach is to mark what genuinely sounds like you in work situations.

items.q: Can I download the test as a PDF and take it on paper?
items.a: Yes. The “{pdf}” page has a free printable file: 24 blocks of statements, the key and scoring table, and descriptions of the 16 profiles. You will have to work out the result by hand; the online version does that for you and draws the chart.

about.title: About — a Free DISC Test in 10 Languages
about.description: Who made this DISC test and why, what it is based on, what it does and what it does not promise.

p: We wanted a DISC test that anyone can take in ten minutes without signing up or paying, get a clear report in their own language and share it with their team. The site works in ten languages, the result appears instantly and arrives by email, and managers and HR have a panel where participants' results are collected into a table.

sections.h: What the test is based on
p: The test is built on William Marston's four-factor model (1928) and later most/least questionnaires: 24 blocks of four statements, one per style. The descriptions of the styles and the sixteen profiles were written by the site's authors on the basis of the generally accepted DISC characteristics and checked for natural language.
The project is independent and not affiliated with Wiley (DiSC®), TTI Success Insights or other trademark holders. The word DISC is used as the generic name of the model.

sections.h: What the test does not promise
p: The test is not a clinical or diagnostic tool, does not measure intelligence, competence or fit for a job, and should not be the sole basis for hiring decisions. It is a starting point for self-observation and team conversation.

You can write to us via the “{contact}” form. The site's source code is open on GitHub: github.com/Man-You-Can/disc-test — that is also the place to report a translation error or suggest an improvement.

privacy.title: Privacy — What Data the DISC Test Uses
privacy.description: What data the DISC test stores, where it is kept, who receives it and how to delete it.

p: Before the test you enter your name and email address. During the test your answers are saved, and after it your result, chosen language and a note that you have seen the cookie notice. All of this is kept in your browser's local storage. When you finish the test, your name, email address, test date and result are also stored in the site owner's results database.

When you finish the test, your name, email address and answers (as a result code) are passed to the email-sending service, a Google Apps Script running in the site owner's Google account. It sends you your result and records your name, email address, test date and result (profile, scores and report link) in the results database, a Google Sheet in the same account. The data is not used for any other purpose and is not passed to third parties.

The hosting provider (GitHub Pages) receives standard technical request data: IP address, browser type, page address. Fonts are served from this site itself and are not loaded from Google's servers. Visit statistics are collected by Yandex Metrica (Yandex LLC): it receives anonymised visit data, namely the page address without the result code, the referrer, device and browser type, and a recording of on-page actions (Webvisor); the name and email fields, the result link and code are excluded from the recording. The data is processed under Yandex's terms; you can stop the collection in your browser settings or with a tracker blocker. No advertising trackers are used.

The report link contains your name, email address and answers in encoded form. Anyone with the link can open the report, so share it only with people you trust. The admin panel works only in the browser of the person who pasted the codes into it.

Messages from the contact form — name, email address, text and attached files — are emailed to {email} via the same Google Apps Script and are used only to reply to you. They are not written to the results database, and the attached files are not stored anywhere except in that email.

To delete the data on your device, clear the site's data in your browser settings or press “Take the test again”. The result email is in your mailbox. To ask for your record in the results database and the sender-side copy of the email to be deleted, contact us via the contact form.

The site itself sets no cookies: for the items above it uses the browser's local storage, a technology with the same purpose. Yandex Metrica sets its own cookies (for example _ym_uid and _ym_d) to tell visitors apart. That is why the notice is shown once on your first visit.
Last updated: 7 September 2026. Changes in how data is handled will be reflected on this page.

results.title: DISC Test Results Explained: How to Read Your Chart and Profile
results.description: How to read your DISC test results: the three chart lines, percentages, dominant and secondary styles, balanced profile. Examples and common mistakes.
results.lead: A DISC test result is not a single letter but a chart with three lines, percentages for the four styles and a one- or two-letter profile. Below we walk through examples of what each element of the report means and how to avoid misreading it.

p: After the last block you see four elements: the profile name with one or two letters (for example, “Pioneer, DI”), a chart with three lines, four scales with percentages, and a written description: traits, strengths, growth areas, motivation, behavior under stress and recommendations on how to communicate with you. The same report is emailed to you and opens by link.

Every number in the report is derived from your marks in the 24 blocks. In each block you chose one statement as “most like me” and one as “least like me”, and each statement belongs to one of the styles D, I, S or C. So each style has two numbers: how many times you chose it as “most” and how many times as “least”.

sections.h: The three lines on the chart
p: The overall profile (the bold line with colored dots) is the main one. It is the difference between the “most” and “least” marks for each style, converted to a scale from 0 to 24. The midpoint of the scale is 12, shown on the chart as a dashed line. A style above the midpoint is considered pronounced; below it, weakly expressed.

The public self is the line based on the “most” marks. It is how you try to behave at work, the image you consciously maintain. The natural self is the line based on the “least” marks, inverted: the less often you rejected a style, the higher the point. It is closer to your effortless behavior, on “autopilot”, for example under pressure or in an unfamiliar situation.

If all three lines follow each other, you behave much the same in any setting. If the public self and the natural self diverge, that isn't a problem but a clue: you switch some style on by an act of will. Most often it means your role requires behavior that doesn't come naturally to you, and that behavior costs you energy.

The dominant style is the one with the highest overall value. It is the first letter of your profile and the basis of the description. A secondary style counts if its value is positive and at least 40% of the dominant one (minimum 3 points on the “raw” scale from −24 to +24). It becomes the second letter and adds a shade to the description: a D with a secondary I (DI) persuades with momentum and enthusiasm, a D with a secondary C (DC) with demands and arguments.

The order of the letters matters: DI and ID are different profiles. In DI the dominant style is Dominance and Influence supports it; in ID the person is first of all sociable and inspiring, and assertiveness switches on when needed. If the second style's value is negative or noticeably lower than the dominant one, the profile stays “pure”: D, I, S or C.

The percentages on the four scales are the same overall value converted to a scale from 0 to 100: −24 corresponds to 0%, 0 to 50%, +24 to 100%. A value above 50% means you chose the style more often than you rejected it; below 50%, the reverse. It isn't “how much D is in me” but a measure of how characteristic the style is for you compared with the other three.

The “raw” values of the four styles always add up to zero: the test compares the styles with one another rather than measuring each separately. So a high result in one style inevitably means a low result in another. The opposites are usually D and S or I and C: they sit at opposite ends of the pace and focus axes.

If no value rises noticeably above the midpoint, the report calls the profile balanced but still names a dominant style based on the highest number. Such a result most often means flexibility: you switch between styles depending on the situation, and colleagues with different styles all find you equally easy to work with.

Less often, a flat chart means you answered hesitantly, thought too long or tried to pick the “right” answers. It is easy to check: take the test again in a few days, answering quickly and with a specific work role in mind. If the profile is flat again, flexibility really is your distinctive trait.

sections.h: What to do with your result
p: Start with the description of your strengths and growth areas: note what you recognize and what seems off. Then read the “How to communicate with you” section and ask yourself whether your colleagues know this. The most useful thing to do with a result is talk about it: compare profiles with your team on the style compatibility page and agree on how to allow for the differences.

A profile is neither a verdict nor a ceiling. It describes your habitual behavior now, and it may shift with a new role, experience and circumstances. It is worth saving the link to your report and retaking the test in a year: the changes will show how your work has shaped you.

sections.h: Common mistakes when reading the result
ul: Treating one style as “the best”. Every style has strengths and a price: D's drive turns into impatience, C's thoroughness into missed deadlines.
Mixing up the order of the letters. DI and ID, SC and CS are different profiles with different dominant styles.
Reading the percentages as shares. 70% in D doesn't mean “70% dominant”; it means you chose the D style noticeably more often than you rejected it.
Drawing conclusions about competence. DISC describes behavioral style, not abilities, intelligence or suitability for a job.
Judging someone by their result. The report is a self-assessment, and the person themselves knows best where the description hits the mark and where it doesn't.

examples.text: The overall profile is high in D and I, low in S and C. The dominant style is Dominance (D); Influence (I) is pronounced and counted as secondary: profile DI, “Pioneer”. This person makes decisions quickly and brings people along, but patience for details and caution often run short.

The mirror image: S and C above the midpoint, D and I below. The dominant style is Steadiness (S), the secondary one Conscientiousness (C): profile SC, “Specialist”. Methodical, reliable and rule-abiding, but abrupt change and pressure are hard to take.

All four values are close to the midpoint. A dominant style is formally assigned by the highest number, but the report notes that the profile is balanced. Most likely this person flexibly changes style with the situation; if the answers were hesitant, it is worth taking the test again.

colors.title: DISC Colors: Red, Yellow, Green and Blue Personality Types
colors.description: Four DISC colors: red (D), yellow (I), green (S), blue (C). What each color means, how to find yours and how color tests differ from DISC. Free online test.
colors.h1: DISC colors: red, yellow, green, blue
colors.lead: The four DISC styles are often labeled with colors: red for Dominance, yellow for Influence, green for Steadiness, blue for Conscientiousness. The colors add nothing to the model, but they make the styles easy to remember and to talk about in a team. Here is what stands behind each color and how to find yours.

D.name: Red
D.text: Red is the color of speed and drive. “Reds” set a goal and go straight for it, decide quickly, argue, take responsibility and aren't afraid of conflict. On a team they push things forward, but they can be overbearing and lose patience with those who work more carefully.

I.name: Yellow
I.text: Yellow is the color of energy and communication. “Yellows” make friends easily, inspire, come up with ideas and spread optimism. Recognition and live contact matter to them; details, deadlines and routine come harder, and promises sometimes outrun what's possible.

S.name: Green
S.text: Green is the color of calm and reliability. “Greens” know how to listen, support others, finish what they start and protect relationships on the team. They need predictability and time to adjust to change; open conflict and pressure are hard for them to bear.

C.name: Blue
C.text: Blue is the color of analysis and order. “Blues” rely on facts, check details, plan and follow standards. They are responsible for quality, but they can get stuck in analysis, stretch deadlines in pursuit of perfection and come across as cold.

p: William Marston, the author of the four-factor model, didn't use colors: his four dimensions were called Dominance, Inducement, Submission and Compliance. The colors came later, when the model began to be explained in training sessions: four letters are harder to remember than four colors, and a color scheme is handy for posters, cards and group discussion.

There is no single standard, but the most common scheme is the one used on this site: red D, yellow I, green S, blue C. The logic is simple: the “warm” colors go to the fast, assertive styles, the “cool” ones to the measured styles. In some systems yellow and green swap places, so when comparing results from different sources, look at the letters, not the colors.

sections.h: Two axes instead of four colors
p: The colors are easier to understand through two axes. The first is pace: red and yellow act fast and decisively, green and blue deliberately and cautiously. The second is focus: red and blue concentrate on tasks and results, yellow and green on people and relationships. Each color is the intersection of two axes, not a separate “breed” of people.

That is why neighboring colors resemble each other while opposites differ the most: red and green (D and S), yellow and blue (I and C). It is between these that misunderstandings arise most often on a team, and it is these that complement each other best once they have agreed on the rules.

Pure colors are rare: most people have two pronounced styles, a dominant and a secondary one, and the test result looks like “red with yellow” (profile DI) or “green with blue” (SC). The test on this site shows the intensity of all four styles in percent and a chart, rather than simply assigning you a color.

You can also estimate your color without the test. You decide quickly and argue for results: probably red. You make friends easily and energize people: yellow. You are patient, reliable and avoid conflict: green. You check every detail and dislike rushing: blue. But an “eyeballed” self-assessment often differs from the test: people tend to attribute to themselves the style that is valued in their environment.

sections.h: Color tests and DISC: what's the difference
p: There are separate “color” typologies, the best known of which is Insights Discovery, with the same set of red, yellow, green and blue. They grew out of Jung's work and differ from DISC in the details: different questions, a different scale, a different interpretation of the shades. Similar color names don't mean the same result.

There are also popular “what color are you” quizzes with a dozen questions. They are fine as entertainment, but they don't distinguish a dominant style from a secondary one, don't show intensity and don't tell you what to do with the result. The 24-block DISC test gives you all of that and remains free.

A color map of the team is a quick way to spot imbalances. A team made up entirely of “reds” makes decisions fast and falls out just as fast; a team of “greens” is close-knit but avoids difficult conversations and puts off change. A mixed team works better when everyone understands what to expect from another color: how to assign a task, how to give feedback, how to argue.

The style compatibility page covers every pair: what they have in common, where friction arises and what each of them can do. And for managers and HR there is a separate guide on how to run the test with a team and discuss the results.

A color is a label, and labels oversimplify. “Well, you're red” sounds like an excuse for rudeness, and “they're green, what do you expect” like giving up on expectations. DISC describes habitual behavior, not character, values or abilities, and any style can be developed. Use the colors to understand each other, not to put people in boxes.

pdf.title: Free Printable DISC Test PDF: Download With Key and Scoring
pdf.description: Free printable DISC test PDF: 24 blocks of statements, key, scoring table, 16 profile descriptions. Print and fill in on paper; the online version scores itself.
pdf.h1: DISC test PDF: download and print
pdf.lead: The same full version of the test as online, but as a printable file: 24 blocks of four statements, the style key, a scoring table and descriptions of all 16 profiles. The file is free and requires no sign-up.

after: The file is in A4 format and in the language of this page. You can print it in black and white: the questionnaire doesn't rely on color.

sections.h: When you need a paper version
p: A paper test is convenient at a training session or strategy offsite where not every participant has a computer, in a class, and anywhere phones aren't allowed. Some people simply find it easier to concentrate on paper: mark, turn the page, no notifications to distract you.

If participants do have their phones, the online version is simpler: it scores the result itself, draws the chart, emails the report and provides a link you can share. For teams there is also an admin panel that collects everyone's results.

sections.h: How to fill in and score the test
p: In each block, mark the one statement that describes you most and the one that describes you least. Answer according to your usual behavior at work and don't overthink it. Then use the key to write the style letters next to your marks, and for each style count the number of “most like me” and “least like me” marks.

The difference between them is the style's total, from −24 to +24. The style with the highest total is dominant; if the second-highest total is positive and at least 40% of the dominant one (minimum 3), it is the secondary style. That gives a one- or two-letter profile, for example D or DI; its description is in the file, and a detailed explanation with examples is on a separate page.

sections.h: A detailed report for your paper result
p: The paper version gives you a profile and a short description. To get the full report with the chart, strengths, growth areas and communication tips, open your profile's page from the list of 16 profiles or take the test online: it takes about ten minutes.

teams.title: DISC Assessment for Teams, Managers and HR: How to Use It at Work
teams.description: How to use DISC with a team: style map, role assignment, conflicts, onboarding, feedback, sales. Run the free test for your whole team and discuss the results.
teams.lead: DISC is usually taken not alone but as a team: to understand why colleagues react differently, agree on communication rules and assign roles sensibly. This page covers how a manager or HR can run the test, read the team map and discuss the results without labels.

p: Most workplace friction isn't about competence but about style: one person wants to decide quickly, another wants to check first; one speaks bluntly, another finds bluntness rude. DISC gives a shared language for such differences: instead of “they're impossible” you get “they're a high D, they need short answers and results”. The differences don't disappear, but they stop being taken as personal dislike.

The second effect is transparent expectations. When everyone knows how best to communicate with them, and it's written in their report, the manager doesn't have to guess: who to give freedom, who to give clear criteria, who to warn about changes in advance and who to thank in public.

sections.h: The team map: what the distribution of styles shows
p: Collect the participants' profiles and look at the proportions. A team dominated by D decides fast and takes risks, but often quarrels and doesn't hear the cautious voices. A surplus of I brings energy and ideas, but deadlines and details suffer. A team of S is close-knit and reliable, but avoids difficult conversations and postpones change. A surplus of C ensures quality, but decisions drag on and anything new is met with skepticism.

Gaps matter more than imbalances. If the team has no pronounced C, there is nobody to check and plan for risks; if there is no I, nobody sells ideas to the outside world and keeps spirits up. That is not a reason to look for the “missing type” when hiring, but a reason to close the gap deliberately: appoint someone responsible for checking or for communication and give them time for it.

ul: A conflict between two colleagues. Most often it is a pair of opposite styles: D and S or I and C. Look the pair up on the compatibility page and suggest one specific change in communication to each of them.
A new hire. A test taken during onboarding tells the mentor how to bring the person into the work: an S needs clear rules and time, a D needs an independent task from day one.

Assigning roles in a project. Launches and negotiations go to those with pronounced D and I; support and quality to those with S and C. This is a guide, not a ban: people cope with “foreign” tasks too, they just spend more energy on them.

Feedback. A C needs facts and time to think, an I needs their contribution acknowledged before any criticism, an S needs a calm one-on-one conversation, a D needs it short and to the point with no preamble.

Sales and negotiation. Identify the client's style from their behavior and speak their language: results and deadlines for a D, relationships and emotions for an I, guarantees and reliability for an S, data and comparisons for a C.

sections.h: How to run the test with your team on this site
ol: Take the test yourself: that way you'll know what participants will see and can show a sample report.

Send your colleagues the link to the site in the language they need. No sign-up is required and the test takes about ten minutes; each person enters their name and email and gets the report on screen and by email.
Ask each person to forward you the link to their result or the code from the report. The result is visible only to whoever has the link; no data is sent to the manager automatically.

Open the admin panel (link in the site footer) and paste in the codes you received. The panel compiles a table with names, profiles and scores; you can copy it into Excel. The table is stored only in your browser.
Schedule a joint meeting: explain the four styles, show the team map and let everyone say what in their report hit the mark and what didn't.

p: The first rule: the result belongs to the participant. Nobody is obliged to show their report, and the discussion starts with the person speaking about themselves. The second: there are no good or bad styles. Every time someone says “D is better for a manager”, remind them of the price of each style and that a team needs all four.

A practical format is one request from each person: “It helps me when…” and “It gets in my way when…”. Such sentences, said out loud and written down, give a team more than any typology. Come back to them in two or three months and check what has changed.

DISC is appropriate in an interview as a topic for talking about work style and as a hint about which questions to ask: for example, how a candidate with a high C copes with uncertainty. But a hiring decision must not be based on a profile: the method describes behavioral preferences, not competence, motivation, experience or fit for the job, and any style can succeed in almost any role.

A separate note on ethics: ask a candidate to take the test only after explaining why it is needed and who will see the result. The test is not a diagnostic tool, and using it to screen people out means losing good people and risking your reputation.

ul: Labeling people: “you're an S, you don't care anyway” turns a tool for understanding into an excuse for neglect.
Expecting the same profile from everyone in a department. Homogeneous teams are blind to what they can't do.
Running the test without a discussion. A report nobody discussed is forgotten within a week.
Publishing results without consent. A profile is personal information, even if it contains nothing hurtful.
Treating a profile as fixed. A year later, in a new role, the result may shift, and that is normal.

mbti.title: DISC vs MBTI vs Big Five: How They Differ and Which to Choose
mbti.description: DISC vs MBTI vs Big Five: what each model measures, how many types, how reliable they are, where they're used and which test to choose. Free DISC test online.
mbti.h1: DISC vs MBTI: what's the difference
mbti.lead: DISC and MBTI are the two best-known typologies in team work, and they are constantly confused. Both give you four letters, both talk about “types”, but they measure different things and answer different questions. Below is a short comparison, including with the Big Five, and practical advice on which to choose.

p: DISC describes observable behavior: how a person acts, communicates and makes decisions, on four scales: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness. The result is a dominant and a secondary style, 16 profiles in all. The model is deliberately simple and focused on work: what you need from colleagues and what they need from you.

MBTI (Myers–Briggs Type Indicator) sorts people into 16 types based on four dichotomies: extraversion vs. introversion, sensing vs. intuition, thinking vs. feeling, judging vs. perceiving. It is a model of preferences in perception and decision-making that grew out of Jung's typology. A type like INTJ or ESFP says how a person takes in information and what matters to them, not how they behave in a meeting.

The Big Five is not a typology but five continuous traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism. It is the scientific standard in personality psychology: it has the best reliability and predictive power, but a result in the form of five scales is harder to turn into practical recommendations.
The table simplifies, but it helps you see the main point: DISC is about behavior, MBTI about preferences, the Big Five about traits.

sections.h: Can you convert MBTI to DISC?
p: There is no exact correspondence, because the models measure different things, but there are statistical links. Extraversion in MBTI more often goes with high D and I, introversion with S and C. A preference for Thinking (T) leans toward D and C, Feeling (F) toward I and S. So an ENTJ often gets a D or DC profile, an ESFP an I or IS, an ISFJ an S or SC, an INTP a C or CD.

Treat this as a rough guide: people with the same MBTI type can show different DISC profiles depending on their role, and a DISC profile is more likely to shift with a change of job than an MBTI type is. If you need to understand how a colleague will behave in a specific situation, their DISC report is more useful than four MBTI letters.

MBTI is criticized because its dichotomies are artificial: most people sit near the middle of the scale, and a small change in answers moves them to a different type. DISC partly avoids this problem because it shows the intensity of the styles rather than assigning you to one of two poles, but it too remains a self-report with moderate reliability. The Big Five is more reliable than both because it doesn't try to divide people into types.

The practical conclusion: neither DISC nor MBTI is suitable as the sole basis for hiring or promotion decisions. But both work well as a language for talking about differences, and here DISC wins on simplicity: four styles can be learned in one meeting, sixteen MBTI types can't.

ul: You need to improve communication on a team, assign roles or prepare for a negotiation: DISC. It is about behavior that others can see, and it gives ready-made “how to communicate with me” recommendations.
You want to understand yourself, where your preferences come from and where to grow: MBTI or the Big Five. They describe inner attitudes in more depth.
You need data for research or a prediction, for example of an employee's dependability: the Big Five. It has the best evidence base.
Not sure? Take DISC: it's ten minutes, free and needs no sign-up, and the result is immediately usable at work.

p: Yes, and it's useful: the models don't contradict each other but complement each other. MBTI will explain why you are more comfortable working with ideas than with people, and DISC will show how that looks to your colleagues and what to do about it. Save both results and compare them: the discrepancies often turn out to be the most interesting findings.

DISC
MBTI
Big Five

24 “most / least like me” blocks, about 10 minutes
Marston's model (1928); moderate reliability, high practicality
Jung (1921), Myers and Briggs (1940s); criticized for poor type reproducibility
Lexical approach and factor analysis; the most thoroughly tested model

compatibility.title: DISC Compatibility Chart: How D, I, S and C Work Together
compatibility.description: DISC style compatibility for every pair: D–I, D–S, D–C, I–S, I–C, S–C and same-style pairs. What they share, where friction arises and what to do. Free test.
compatibility.lead: There are no incompatible pairs in DISC: any two styles can work together if they understand their differences. But every pair has its own strengths and its own typical conflicts. Pick two styles in the chart to find out what they have in common, where friction arises and what each of them can do.

p: Compatibility here isn't “are you right for each other” but how easily two styles understand each other without effort. Neighboring styles (D and I, I and S, S and C, C and D) share one axis, pace or focus, and usually find common ground quickly. Opposites (D and S, I and C) differ on both axes: they have the hardest time, but they also complement each other the most.

Matching styles understand each other instantly, but they amplify their shared weaknesses: two Ds fight over the wheel, two Ss put off change for years. So an “easy” pair isn't always a “strong” one, and a difficult pair that has agreed on rules gets the best result.

Identify both people's dominant styles: your own from the test, the other person's from the test or from observation. Open the pair's page and read both sets of tips, yours and theirs. The most useful thing is to go through the page together and each pick one rule you are willing to follow. If either of you has a pronounced secondary style, look at its pair too: it will explain some of the behavior that doesn't fit the dominant style.

DD.summary: Two people used to deciding and leading. Together they move things fast, but they fight for control and rarely give way.
DD.text: A D and D pair means speed and clarity: both speak directly, neither takes offense at directness in return, both decide quickly and can't stand drawn-out discussions. The trouble starts when there can be only one decision. Each is sure of their own view, both are used to winning, and an argument about the work easily turns into a fight over who's in charge. For the pair to work, areas of responsibility need to be divided in advance.
common: Focus on results and deadlines
Straight talk without hints or hurt feelings
Willingness to take responsibility and risks
friction: A struggle for control and the last word
Impatience: both interrupt and rush
Nobody checks the details or listens to the cautious

D: Agree on who is responsible for what, and stay out of each other's territory
Argue about the criteria for the result, not about who is right
Bring an S or a C into the discussion: they see what you both miss

DI.summary: The most energetic pair: D sets the goal and the pace, I fires people up. Together they launch projects, but tend to underestimate details and caution.
DI.text: D and I share a fast pace: both decide on the go, love challenges and can't stand routine. The difference is focus: D thinks about results, I about people and impressions. It's a happy complement: D provides direction and toughness, I provides contacts, morale and the ability to sell an idea. Friction arises when D sees I's talkativeness as a waste of time, and I finds D cold and abrupt. Both should remember that behind their energy, someone has to keep an eye on the details.
common: A fast pace and readiness to act without long preparation
Optimism and an appetite for new tasks
A dislike of routine and micromanagement
friction: D demands specifics, I gets carried away with conversation
I is hurt by bluntness, D is irritated by emotions
Both are overoptimistic about deadlines and miss details

D: Start the conversation with two minutes about the person, then get down to business
Acknowledge I's contribution out loud: for them it's fuel
Don't cut ideas off mid-flight: let them finish, then pick the best
I: Keep it short with a D: the result, the deadline, what you need from them
Put agreements in writing so enthusiasm doesn't drift away from the facts
Don't take D's directness personally: it's a style, not a judgment

DS.summary: Opposites on both axes: D is fast and results-driven, S is measured and protects relationships. The hardest pair and one of the most useful.
DS.text: D and S differ in everything: pace, attitude to conflict, what counts as important. D sees slowness and indecision in S; S sees pressure and disrespect in D. And yet the pair complements each other perfectly: D breaks through and launches, S holds on, sees things through and keeps the team together. It only works with explicit rules: D eases off the pressure and gives warning of changes, S learns to say “no” and to voice disagreement out loud rather than through silence.
common: Practicality: both want the job done
Loyalty to commitments
A dislike of empty talk and posturing
friction: Pace: D rushes, S needs time
Conflict: D takes it on easily, S avoids it at all costs
S silently agrees and doesn't do it, D reads that as sabotage

D: Give advance warning of changes and explain why they're needed
Ask for their opinion directly and wait for the answer without filling the pause
Thank them for their reliability: an S won't ask for recognition
S: Voice disagreement right away, briefly and to the point: a D respects that
Ask for clear deadlines and priorities instead of guessing
Don't take D's drive as hostility: it's just their normal speed

DC.summary: Both are task- and results-oriented, but D wants it fast and C wants it right. A strong pair for complex projects, once they agree on pace.
DC.text: D and C share a focus on the task: for both, the work matters more than the atmosphere, both value competence and don't waste time on small talk. The difference is pace: D decides with half the data, C wants to gather everything and check it. D sees C as a brake and an over-cautious worrier; C sees D as irresponsible. On a complex project this is the best combination: D keeps things moving, C provides quality and protection from mistakes. The key is to decide in advance where speed is needed and where precision.
common: Focus on the task and the result, not on relationships
Respect for competence and logic
Directness: both prefer facts to emotions
friction: D decides fast, C demands data and time
C reads drive as pressure, D reads caution as sabotage
Both are critical and stingy with recognition

D: Give C time to analyze, and say in advance when you need an answer
Back your decisions with facts, not “because I said so”
Divide the tasks: where the cost of a mistake is high, C has the last word
C: Offer D a “good enough now” option instead of “perfect later”
Report risks briefly, with an assessment of the consequences, without lengthy justification
Don't wait for praise from a D: the absence of criticism is their approval

II.summary: Two people who love people, ideas and attention. Together they have fun and things come easily, but someone has to watch the deadlines and details.
II.text: An I and I pair means energy, optimism and a stream of ideas. They find common ground quickly, support each other and create an atmosphere around them that people want to work in. The problems come from outside: promises made, deadlines forgotten, details nobody checked. Another trap is competing for attention: both want to be center stage, and the conversation turns into two monologues. Such a pair needs an external anchor: written agreements, a calendar and a colleague with a pronounced C or S.
common: Sociability and ease of contact
Optimism and faith in ideas
A dislike of formalities and routine
friction: Both talk, nobody listens
Promises without a plan: deadlines and details slip
Conflicts are hushed up to keep the mood good

I: End every meeting with a list: who, what, by when
Split the roles: one leads the conversation, the other takes notes
Ask a C or an S to check the plan before you announce it

IS.summary: A warm and friendly pair: I inspires, S supports. Good for atmosphere and clients, worse for hard decisions.
IS.text: I and S share a focus on people: relationships, atmosphere and recognition matter to both. The difference is pace: I is fast, spontaneous and loves novelty, S is measured and prefers the familiar order. Together they create the friendliest environment on the team, but they struggle with tough decisions, avoid unpleasant conversations and can let a problem drag on just to avoid hurting anyone. I can nudge S toward change; S can hold I back from impulsive promises.
common: Attention to people and relationships
A desire for harmony and a good atmosphere
Readiness to help and support
friction: I changes plans on the fly, which throws S off balance
Both avoid conflict, and problems pile up
I talks a lot, S gives way and keeps quiet about their own needs

I: Warn S about changes in advance and don't change decisions without reason
Ask for S's opinion directly: they won't push it on you
Finish what you start: S values reliability above ideas
S: State your boundaries out loud: an I won't guess them
Support I's ideas, but ask for a plan and deadlines
Don't be afraid of honest feedback: an I will take it better than you think

IC.summary: Opposites: I lives on people and impressions, C on facts and precision. A difficult pair that becomes a strong one once there is trust.
IC.text: I and C differ on both axes: pace and focus. I talks a lot, decides fast and relies on feeling; C talks little, decides after checking and relies on data. To C, I seems superficial; to I, C seems tedious and cold. Yet together they cover each other completely: I sells, inspires and negotiates, C makes sure what was promised actually works. The condition is mutual respect: I acknowledges the value of checking, C acknowledges the value of contact.
common: An interest in ideas, even if from different angles
A desire to do things well: I beautifully, C correctly
No power struggle: neither needs control for its own sake
friction: I promises, C checks and finds discrepancies
C needs quiet and time, I needs interaction and speed
I's emotionality irritates C, C's reserve wounds I

I: Prepare facts and figures before talking to a C
Allow time for an answer: C's silence is thinking, not refusal
Don't take criticism of the details as rejection of the idea
C: Start by acknowledging the idea, then move on to the risks
Explain your conclusions in plain words, without listing all the data
Sometimes settle for “good enough”: not every detail is worth an argument

SS.summary: The calmest pair: reliability, patience and mutual support. The danger is stagnation and a reluctance to raise difficult topics.
SS.text: Two Ss understand each other without words: both value stability, keep their promises, listen and don't push. Such a pair can work steadily and without conflict for years. The flip side is avoiding anything that disturbs the peace: change, arguments, unpleasant conversations. Problems aren't solved but endured; decisions are postponed because nobody wants to take the initiative first. An S and S pair benefits from an outside push: firm deadlines, a manager with D or a colleague with I who will stir things up.
common: Reliability and consistency
Patience and the ability to listen
Loyalty to the team and the familiar way of doing things
friction: Nobody starts changes or takes the initiative
Disagreement is hushed up, resentment builds
Decisions are postponed while each waits for the other to decide

S: Set deadlines for each other: without them nothing moves
Agree to name problems out loud, even small ones
Take turns being “the one who decides”

SC.summary: A measured and thorough pair: S holds the relationships, C holds the quality. Excellent for support work and processes, hard on change.
SC.text: S and C share a measured pace: neither likes rushing, both value order and predictability and think their steps through. The difference is focus: S thinks about people and harmony, C about rules and facts. Together they build the most stable processes on the team, but they struggle to accept anything new, and they go through change together and slowly. The typical conflict is a quiet one: C criticizes mistakes and seems callous to S; S bends the rules for people's sake and seems lax to C.
common: Caution and well-considered decisions
Respect for order and agreements
An aversion to haste, chaos and pressure
friction: C puts rules above relationships, S the other way around
Both resist change, and the team stands still
S takes C's criticism as personal coldness

S: Take C's remarks as care for quality, not as being about you
Ask them to explain the logic of a rule rather than arguing with the rule itself
Propose changes in small steps: it's easier for both you and C
C: Soften criticism: first what's good, then what to fix
Remember that for an S, the atmosphere is part of the result
Notice S's contribution out loud: they won't ask for recognition

CC.summary: A pair of experts: precision, logic and high standards. Together they do flawless work, but slowly, and they tend to argue over trifles.
CC.text: Two Cs speak the same language: facts, criteria, risks. They respect each other's competence and produce work nobody can fault. The problem is pace and perfectionism: every detail gets discussed, every decision is postponed until there is complete certainty, and an argument over a comma can drag on for a week. Another trap is reserve: neither talks about tension, and disagreements turn into cold silence. Such a pair needs an external deadline and an agreement that “good enough” is acceptable too.
common: High quality standards
Reliance on data and logic
Discipline and keeping to agreements
friction: Perfectionism doubles, deadlines slip away
Arguments about details with no decision on the substance
Tension goes unspoken and builds up

C: Decide in advance what level of quality is sufficient, and stop there
Limit the time for analysis: a decision on time beats a perfect one with no deadline
Talk about disagreements directly: silence doesn't resolve anything

p: The site is run by the disc-test.org editorial team: we write the texts, maintain the code and answer the mail. The project is independent and non-commercial: the test is free, with no sign-up, no ads and no paid “extended reports”, and the source code is open. We do not sell training or certifications, and we are not affiliated with Wiley (DiSC®), TTI Success Insights or other trademark holders.

We are responsible for everything published on the site. If you find a mistake in the text, an inaccurate translation or a discrepancy between the description of the method and the way the score is actually calculated, write to us: we will fix it and update the date of the change.

sections.h: How we write and check our texts
p: The statements about the method rest on primary sources and peer-reviewed research, including critical work; the list of works is collected in the “{sources}” section. We do not paraphrase commercial reports: the descriptions of the four styles and the sixteen profiles were written by our editorial team on the basis of the generally accepted characteristics of the model.

The source language of the site is Russian. The translations into nine languages were produced with language models and are checked automatically: a script makes sure that the structure of the texts, the terms and the numbers match across all languages. Proofreading by native speakers is planned but has not been done yet, so the translations may still have rough edges.

Every page carries the date it was last updated. We revise the texts when the test itself changes or when readers point something out, and we do not publish anything we cannot back up with a source or with our own checking.

ui.consent.text: This site keeps your progress, result and chosen language in your browser's local storage, and Yandex Metrica collects anonymised visit statistics and a recording of on-page actions to help us improve the site. Your name, email and result are not sent to Metrica.
ui.consent.details: Stored in your browser: the name and email you enter before the test; your answers and unfinished progress; your latest result; your chosen language; a note that you have seen this notice. This data stays on your device and is removed when you clear the site's data. The hosting provider (GitHub Pages) receives standard technical request data. When you finish the test, your name, email and answers are passed to the email-sending service (Google Apps Script), which emails you your result and stores your name, email, date and result in the site owner's results database (a Google Sheet). Yandex Metrica (Yandex LLC) receives the page address without the result code, the referrer, device and browser type, an anonymised recording of on-page actions (the name and email fields, the result link and code are excluded), and sets its own cookies. You can block it in your browser settings or with a tracker blocker. No advertising trackers are used.
ui.print.title: DISC Test — Printable Version
ui.print.name: Name
ui.print.howText: Each block has four statements. In the “+” column, mark the one statement that describes you most; in the “−” column, mark the one that describes you least. Answer according to your usual behavior at work and don't overthink it: your first reaction is the most accurate. There are no right or wrong answers.
ui.print.keyTitle: Key: which style each statement belongs to
ui.print.keyText: For each block, the key shows which style statements 1, 2, 3 and 4 belong to, in the order they appear. Write the style letter next to each of your marks.
ui.print.countText: For each style, count the number of “most like me” marks and the number of “least like me” marks, then subtract the second from the first. The total ranges from −24 to +24, and the totals of the four styles add up to zero.
ui.print.decodeText: The dominant style is the one with the highest total. If the second-highest total is positive and at least 40% of the dominant one (minimum 3 points), it is the secondary style. A profile is written as one letter (for example, D) or two (for example, DI: dominant D, secondary I). If no total is above 2, the profile is balanced: the styles are expressed about equally.
